newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE - Bamboo is secret of Asia's master builder.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Bamboo is secret of Asia's master builder.

text.p: It looks like a construction miracle. Rickety-looking bamboo scaffolding, in a bizarre mix of ancient and modern, veils the ceaseless construction of Hong Kong's new skyscrapers.
For centuries China's symbol of strength and flexibility, bamboo now helps in forging Hong Kong as the world's greatest building site, along with Berlin and Shanghai.
You can use bamboo for graceful furniture and art, you can eat the shoots soaked in oil, and in some hands it delivers deadly blows.

And you can build with it faster and cheaper than Western techniques. Booming East Asia's master builders use bamboo scaffolding that looks frail, yet has a steely strength supporting the rise of concrete-and-glass towers.
In Hong Kong you can learn the craft from the masters of a tradition that made old China's cities a world wonder, long before Europe's Renaissance recovery from the Dark Ages.
Bamboo scaffolding and the armies of hard-hatted workers who clamber over it are as much a fixture of Hong Kong as the unrivalled neon-lit skyline they help to create.

Cheung Choi, 61, is a Bamboo Master. After crafting bamboo scaffolding in Hong Kong for 47 years, he now shares his expertise with students at the Construction Industry Training Authority (CITA), the only place in Hong Kong where students can learn the art in a structured setting.
Students literally hang on his every word as they dangle fearlessly above his tanned, weathered face, heeding his calls to, "Tie the knot now!" and "Be Careful!".

Traditionally passed from teacher to apprentice on a building site, future scaffolders can now hone their craft in an 11-month training program at CITA studying under, or above, Choi and two other bamboo masters who teach at the school.
FROM MASTER TO APPRENTICE A SECRET ART
Bamboo-scaffolding students typically begin the CITA course at the age of 14, where they learn secrets of the trade that seems to lie in the knot.
The black plastic strips used to tie bamboo poles together look more like decorative ribbon than the key to a modern skyscraper.
Known as "poor man's timber" throughout Asia, instructors at CITA disregard that stigma and consider it often superior to its metal counterpart.
"It is strong. It goes up fast and it's cheap," chief CITA instructor Michael Kan says of the unlikely material. "Metal scaffolding needs very little skill. You use much simpler calculations.
"With bamboo, the craftsman is the engineer. There is no blueprint, no design. All the designs are in the brain of the craftsman."
A CENTURIES OLD MATERIAL, AS STRONG AS IT IS RICKETY
According to Kan, the Chinese have been using bamboo in construction for more than 500 years.
Despite its ability to grow just about anywhere on earth, bamboo for scaffolding, as strong as it appears rickety, is predominantly a Chinese phenomenon. CITA imports its bamboo from China.
Viewed as a weed in many Western nations, bamboo is truly a botanical Rambo. Pillage through a bamboo crop and some environmentalists will applaud you.
As one of the fastest growing woody plants on earth, it cannot be stopped. A grove of bamboo survived the 1945 atomic blast in Hiroshima, miraculously sprouting new shoots in the aftermath.

As Hong Kong grows, with developers unveiling ambitious land reclamation projects, Choi and Kan are optimistic about the future of bamboo scaffolding and the next generations they are grooming as craftsmen.
"It's not easy." said Kan. "But after studying with Mr Choi, they know how to do it."
